newsitem.title: USA: IMM currency futures close higher across the board.
newsitem.headline: IMM currency futures close higher across the board.

text.p: IMM currency futures closed higher across the board, as funds and dealers continued to liquidate long dollar positions, traders and analysts said.
While March marks backtracked from the daily high of $0.6005, the contract held above $0.5970 -- a level that corresponds to key support of 1.6770 in the dollar/mark rate.
The 1.6770 level was the upper end of the spot rate's range before the last Group of Seven meeting, one analyst noted.
"Since breaking through that level, we've never traded below it until last night," said John Nelson, forex trading manager at ABN AMRO Bank in Chicago.
He said the dollar/mark's failure to rally through 1.6770 after retesting that level in U.S. dealings points to further U.S. dollar declines in the short term.
"The medium-term trend is higher," he said. "The dollar could fall one percent to 1.6550 and the longer-term trend would still be intact."
Many analysts said the dollar would consolidate ahead of the first leg of U.S. Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan's testimony to Congress on Wednesday.
"This is just a respite from consistent depreciation," Nelson said about the Swiss franc's rally.
Greenspan will speak to the Senate Banking Committee on Wednesday. The second leg of Greenspan's testimony was changed to Wednesday, March 5, from Thursday, February 27.
Nelson said mark's rally was not built on concerns about the fate of European monetary union, noting that the cash mark's performance on the crosses was subdued.
"If anything a delay in the EMU would be a call to buy dollars," he said. "Initially, you would see a move to buy marks, but it would bode well for the dollar longer term."
However, concerns about the fate of a single European currency were attributed to the rally in sterling futures.
March sterling extended gains late to $1.6360, near the 100-day moving average of $1.6364.
March yen trimmed gains in what a floor trader called "a return to reasonable levels."
"The question was why were we so high in the first place," he said, referring to March yen's rise to $0.008245.

Many analysts attributed yen's rise to Japanese repatriation ahead of Japan's fiscal year-end on March 31. Some said repatriation could be even heavier than usual this year due to concerns about Japan's financial service sector.

At the end of pit trade, March yen rose $0.000074 to $0.008211, marks were up $0.0056 to $0.5985, Swiss francs were up $0.0064 to $0.6874, sterling rose $0.0170 to $1.6342, Canadian dollars were up $0.0005 to $0.7348, and Australian dollars were up $0.0005 to $0.7782.
